title: Given the root of a binary tree and two nodes, find their lowest common ancestor, which is the deepest node that has both target nodes as descendants.
shortTitle: Lowest Common Ancestor — recursive: if left and right both non-null, current is LCA

s1_definition.profdef: The Lowest Common Ancestor of two nodes is the deepest node whose subtree contains both of them. The recursive solution searches the tree once: if the current node is either target it returns itself, and otherwise it recurses into both children; if both sides return a non-null result, the current node is the lowest common ancestor, and if only one side does, that side's result bubbles up.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh and Priya work in different teams of the bank, and HR wants the lowest-level manager who oversees both of them. Starting from the top, each manager asks: is either of these two people found in my left team, my right team, or am I one of them? If one target is found on the left and the other on the right, this manager is the lowest common boss. If both are found on the same side, the answer lies deeper on that side.
s1_definition.oneliner: Recurse both sides; if each side finds one target, the current node is the lowest common ancestor, otherwise pass up whichever side found something.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Lowest Common Ancestor of two nodes is the deepest node whose subtree contains both of them. The recursive solution searches the tree once: if the current node is either target it returns itself, and otherwise it recurses into both children; if both sides return a non-null result, the current node is the lowest common ancestor, and if only one side does, that side's result bubbles up.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh and Priya work in different teams of the bank, and HR wants the lowest-level manager who oversees both of them. Starting from the top, each manager asks: is either of these two people found in my left team, my right team, or am I one of them? If one target is found on the left and the other on the right, this manager is the lowest common boss. If both are found on the same side, the answer lies deeper on that side.

**One line to remember:** Recurse both sides; if each side finds one target, the current node is the lowest common ancestor, otherwise pass up whichever side found something.

sections.s2_technical:
The elegance of this algorithm is that a single post-order traversal answers the question without storing paths. Each recursive call returns a node that signals what it found in its subtree.

The base case returns the current node if it is null or if it equals either target. For example: `if (node == null || node == p || node == q) return node;`. Returning the target itself is the signal that this subtree contains a target.

The recursive case searches both children. For example: `Node left = lca(node.left, p, q); Node right = lca(node.right, p, q);`.

The decision is based on what the two sides report. If both left and right returned non-null, it means one target was found in each subtree, so the current node is their lowest common ancestor. For example: `if (left != null && right != null) return node;`. If only one side returned non-null, both targets are in that subtree, so you propagate that result upward. For example: `return (left != null) ? left : right;`.

The time complexity is linear because the tree is visited once, and the space is proportional to the height from the recursion stack. A senior nuance concerns the common assumption that both targets exist in the tree; if one might be absent, the simple version could return the present node as if it were the ancestor, so a stricter version continues searching and confirms both were actually found before declaring an ancestor. Another nuance is that for a binary search tree you do not need this general algorithm; you can use the ordering to walk down in height-time, going left when both targets are smaller and right when both are larger, and the split point is the ancestor.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the approval hierarchy is a tree, and for a conflict-of-interest check the compliance team must find the lowest-level manager who oversees both of two employees involved in a transaction. That manager is the one accountable for the conflict. This is exactly how Lowest Common Ancestor works — it finds the deepest shared ancestor.

Problem 2 — The check must work for any pair, whether one is an ancestor of the other or they sit in separate branches. This is exactly why the recursion handles the case where a target is itself the ancestor by returning the node when it is encountered.

The mini-project builds an `EmployeeNode` class, an `OrgLcaService` with the recursive LCA and logging, and a runnable demo that finds the common manager for two employees.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the org tree and the two targets Rajesh and Priya.

Step 1: The call starts at CEO. CEO is neither Rajesh nor Priya, so it searches both children.

Step 2: It recurses into RegionHead. RegionHead is neither target, so it searches its children. It recurses into Rajesh, who equals one target, so that call returns Rajesh. It recurses into Priya, who equals the other target, so that call returns Priya.

Step 3: Back at RegionHead, the left returned Rajesh and the right returned Priya, both non-null. One target was found on each side, so RegionHead is their lowest common ancestor and the call returns RegionHead.

Step 4: It recurses into CEO's right child AuditHead. AuditHead is neither target and has no children, so both its recursive calls return null, and AuditHead returns null.

Step 5: Back at CEO, the left returned RegionHead, non-null, and the right returned null. Only one side found something, so CEO propagates the left result, RegionHead, upward. The answer is RegionHead.

Step 6: For the second query, Rajesh and AuditHead, Rajesh is found in the left subtree under RegionHead and AuditHead is found in the right subtree directly under CEO, so both sides of CEO return non-null and CEO itself is the lowest common ancestor.

```text
2026-10-26T18:40:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Conflict-of-Interest Common Manager
2026-10-26T18:40:00Z [INFO] Lowest common manager of Rajesh and Priya is RegionHead
2026-10-26T18:40:00Z [INFO] Lowest common manager of Rajesh and AuditHead is CEO
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
              CEO
            /      \
      RegionHead   AuditHead
       /     \
    Rajesh  Priya

  lca(CEO): left=lca(RegionHead), right=lca(AuditHead)
    lca(RegionHead): left=Rajesh, right=Priya
       both non-null → return RegionHead
    lca(AuditHead): null,null → null
  CEO: left=RegionHead, right=null → propagate RegionHead ★

  Query (Rajesh, AuditHead):
    RegionHead returns Rajesh (left), AuditHead returns itself (right)
    CEO: both non-null → CEO is LCA ★
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Lowest Common Ancestor ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Post-order recursive DFS (children before decision)      │
  │  Return-value signaling (target found bubbles up)         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: EmployeeNode holds structure; Service finds LCA       │
  │  O: BST variant swappable (ordering-based descent)        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   OrgLcaService                       │
  │  + lca(node, p, q): EmployeeNode      │ O(n) time, O(h) stack
  │  + findCommonManager(root,p,q)        │ + logging
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Decision at each node:
    node==null||node==p||node==q → return node
    left && right non-null       → return node (the LCA)
    else                         → return the non-null side

  Contract: assumes p and q exist; returns deepest shared ancestor.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Lowest Common Ancestor of two nodes is the deepest node whose subtree contains both of them, and the recursive solution is elegant because a single post-order traversal answers it without ever storing explicit paths. Each recursive call returns a node that signals what its subtree found. The base case returns the current node if it is null or if it is one of the two targets, and returning the target itself is the signal that this subtree contains a target.

For an internal node, I recurse into both children and then decide based on what they report. If both the left and right calls return something non-null, it means one target was found in each subtree, so the current node is their lowest common ancestor. If only one side returns non-null, both targets live in that subtree, so I propagate that result upward. This clean three-way decision is the whole algorithm.

The complexity is linear with space proportional to the height. I always flag the assumption that both targets exist; if one might be absent, the simple version can mistakenly return the present node, so a stricter variant confirms both were actually found before declaring an ancestor. I also mention that for a binary search tree this general algorithm is unnecessary, because the ordering lets me walk down in height-time, turning left when both targets are smaller and right when both are larger, and the point where they split is the ancestor.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used this in a conflict-of-interest check. The approval hierarchy is a tree, and for two employees involved in the same transaction we need the lowest-level manager who oversees both, because that manager is accountable for the conflict. The recursion handles both the case where the two sit in separate branches and the case where one is itself the other's manager, returning the correct accountable node in a single pass.
